sources: Alaska Department of Fish and Game, Aggressive Moose: "more people in Alaska are injured by moose than by bears each year"; a charging moose often kicks forward with its front hooves; unlike with bears, running from a moose is usually a good idea because it will not chase very far; if knocked down, do not move until the moose moves a safe distance away; https://www.adfg.alaska.gov/index.cfm?adfg=livewith.aggressivemoose

U.S. National Park Service, Moose Safety (Kenai Fjords): if a moose knocks you down, curl up in a ball, protect your head with your arms and keep still; https://www.nps.gov/kefj/planyourvisit/moose-safety.htm
title: Moose Injure More People Than Bears in Alaska 🫎 (Would Meatball Survive? #2)
description:
Would you survive a moose? Alaska's Department of Fish and Game says more people in Alaska are injured by moose than by bears each year. A charging moose often kicks forward with its front hooves. Unlike with bears, running is usually a good idea because a moose won't chase you very far, and if one knocks you down, curl up, protect your head and hold still until it moves away.

#shorts #moose #alaska #wouldmeatballsurvive #meatballmyths

Sources: Alaska Department of Fish and Game (Aggressive Moose); U.S. National Park Service (Moose Safety). General information, not safety training.
